---
title: "Setup your machine for data science with R & Python"
subtitle: "A short guide to getting a fresh machine ready for the courses"
format: html
---

These guidelines are meant to be
followed during the live setup block at the start of the term, but also works
standalone if you come to class with an already-configured machine (skip ahead). 
We target **latest stable** versions of everything. If you are on Linux, see
the dedicated [Ubuntu section](#linux-ubuntu) first: it slightly reshapes the
steps below.

## 1. Install R

R is the language itself. Download the installer for your OS and follow the
instructions:

- macOS / Windows: <https://cran.r-project.org>
- Linux (Ubuntu): follow the [Ubuntu section](#linux-ubuntu) below rather than
  using the generic link.

Check it works:

```r
R.version.string   # e.g. "R version 4.6.1"
```

## 2. Install Quarto

Quarto is our open-source scientific and technical publishing system. It turns
`.qmd` documents (and RevealJS slides!) into polished HTML, PDF, and more.

- Download: <https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/>

Check it works:

```bash
quarto --version   # e.g. 1.10.x
```

## 3. Install Positron (the IDE)

Positron is a next-generation data science IDE (a data-science-flavoured fork
of VS Code) that runs both R and Python.

- Download: <https://positron.posit.co/download.html>
- Choose the arm64 / x86_64 build that matches your machine.

Open Positron. On first launch it will offer to install the R extensions and
detect your R installation. Confirm both.

Positron will use this Quarto automatically for the Quarto preview/render.

## 4. Linux (Ubuntu)

If you run Ubuntu, install the three applications above from their `.deb`
binaries, then set up R packages. Two routes are available for packages: the
fast, recommended **r2u** binaries, or a manual compile-from-source fallback.
Both are detailed below.

### 4.1 Install R, Quarto and Positron from `.deb` files

Download the `.deb` installer for each of R, Quarto and Positron from their
respective sites (choose the arm64 build on an ARM, Apple-Silicon-style
machine, or x86_64 otherwise). Then install them together and let `apt` pull in
any missing dependencies:

```bash
sudo dpkg -i ~/Downloads/*.deb     # adjust the path to where you saved the files
sudo apt --fix-broken install
```

The second command is the important clean-up step: `dpkg -i` itself does not
install dependency packages, so it will often report missing dependencies,
which `apt --fix-broken install` then resolves. If you prefer, a plain `sudo
apt install -f` works the same.

For **R alone** you do not have to use the CRAN `.deb` at all. If you prefer
your package manager, install `r-base` (and `r-base-dev`) from the Ubuntu or
CRAN apt repository afterwards with `sudo apt install r-base r-base-dev`
instead. Either way you do not need RStudio: Positron is the IDE, and it talks
to whatever `R` binary sits on your `PATH`.

### 4.2 Recommended: install R packages via r2u (Ubuntu binaries)

[r2u](https://github.com/eddelbuettel/r2u) is a project that builds almost all
of CRAN (currently about 25,000 packages) into Ubuntu binary `.deb` packages
and serves them as an `apt` repository. With a small companion called
[`bspm`](https://cloud.r-project.org/package=bspm), your ordinary
`install.packages("tidyverse")` transparently installs prebuilt Ubuntu
binaries in seconds, with no compilation and no manual wiring of system
libraries. This removes precisely the `libcurl`/`fontconfig`/`harfbuzz`…
laundry list that makes a source install painful.

Scope and caveats:

- It targets Ubuntu LTS releases (22.04 "jammy", 24.04 "noble", 26.04
  "resolute") on amd64, with arm64 supported on 24.04 and 26.04. It is not for
  other distributions.
- Installing via `bspm` needs `sudo`: it writes into the system R library.
- `renv`-based projects (used later in the Reproducible Workflows course) do
  *not* go through `bspm`; they compile from source. So keep the build tools
  from the fallback below even if you use r2u.

Set it up (condensed from the [official guide](https://eddelbuettel.github.io/r2u/)):

```bash
# 1. fetch the signing key
sudo apt update
sudo apt install --yes --no-install-recommends wget ca-certificates gnupg
gpg --homedir /tmp --no-default-keyring \
    --keyring /usr/share/keyrings/r2u.gpg \
    --keyserver keyserver.ubuntu.com \
    --recv-keys A1489FE2AB99A21A 67C2D66C4B1D4339 51716619E084DAB9

# 2. register the r2u apt repository (adjust 'noble' to your Ubuntu release:
#    jammy, noble or resolute; use `lsb_release -cs` to print it)
echo "deb [signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/r2u.gpg] https://r2u.stat.illinois.edu/ubuntu noble main" \
    | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/r2u.list
sudo apt update

# 3. python pieces bspm needs, then bspm itself
sudo apt install --yes --no-install-recommends python3-{dbus,gi,apt}
sudo Rscript -e 'install.packages("bspm")'

# 4. enable bspm for every R session
sudo bash -c 'echo "suppressMessages(bspm::enable())" >> "$(R RHOME)/etc/Rprofile.site"'
```

From then on, inside Positron's R console, the normal command just works and
pulls binaries:

```r
install.packages("tidyverse")
library(tidyverse)
```

### 4.3 Fallback: compile from source

Use this route if your Ubuntu release is not covered by r2u, you do not want a
system-wide (sudo) install, or a package you need is not in r2u. Compiling the
tidyverse from source needs both a C/C++ toolchain and the header files of the
system libraries several of its packages link against. Install them all at
once:

```bash
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y \
  r-base r-base-dev cmake \
  libcurl4-openssl-dev libssl-dev libxml2-dev libfontconfig1-dev \
  libharfbuzz-dev libfribidi-dev libfreetype6-dev libpng-dev \
  libjpeg-dev
```

(on 24.04 "noble" the JPEG/TIFF library is `libtiff6-dev`; on 22.04 "jammy"
and older it is `libtiff5-dev`, so append the one matching your release).

Then, still in the terminal, install **pak** (a modern, fast package manager
that also helps resolve these build issues) and use it from the R console:

```bash
sudo Rscript -e 'install.packages("pak")'
```

```r
pak::pak("tidyverse")
library(tidyverse)
```

Unlike the r2u path (4.2) where plain `install.packages()` pulls prebuilt
binaries, here pak actually compiles from source, but it does the dependency
bookkeeping for you and caches the compiled result, so a later
reinstallation is quick.

## 5. Install R packages

Open the R console in Positron and run:

```r
install.packages("tidyverse")   # the core data-science collection
```

On Ubuntu with r2u set up (section 4.2), this command automatically installs
Ubuntu binaries, so you do not need `pak` or the manual toolchain. On
macOS/Windows the installer handles everything for you.

A note on the two commands you will meet in this guide:

- `install.packages()` is the R-basics installer. With r2u (`+bspm`) running it
  installs Ubuntu binaries, which is why it is the default here.
- `pak::pak()` is an optional third-party package manager with better
  dependency resolution and caching, and can also install straight from GitHub
  or a local folder. It does **not** go through r2u, so on the r2u path it
  offers no speed advantage. Reach for it when a package is not (yet) on CRAN,
  or to compile from source as in the fallback (section 4.3).

Verify with:

```r
library(tidyverse)
```

You should see the package startup message listing dplyr, tidyr, ggplot2,
readr, purrr, tibble, stringr, forcats.

By the time of the Reproducible Workflows course you will additionally want:

```r
install.packages(c("janitor", "naniar", "skimr", "renv", "knitr", "rmarkdown", "pins"))
```

(`renv` is used for dependency pinning; `pins` for data pinning; `janitor`/`naniar`/`skimr` feed the
data-cleaning and EDA labs. All of these are available as r2u binaries too, so the same plain
`install.packages()` call above works unchanged on the r2u path.)

## 6. Some worthy Positron extensions (optional)

- **Air**: A Visual Studio Code extension for [Air](https://posit-dev.github.io/air/), an R formatter and language server, written in Rust.
- **Jarl**: A Visual Studio Code extension for [Jarl](https://jarl.etiennebacher.com), a fast R linter.
- **Posit Assistant**: An AI assistant for Positron. It uses functionality that is available only in Positron, so it will not work with other VS Code forks, like Cursor or Windsurf.
- **Pyrefly**: The Pyrefly extension uses Pyrefly to provide language server features for Python in VS Code. Please see <https://pyrefly.org> for more information.
- **Quarto**: A Visual Studio Code extension for the [Quarto](https://quarto.org) scientific and technical publishing system.
- **Quarto Wizard**: A Visual Studio Code extension that helps you manage your Quarto projects. It allows you to easily install Quarto extensions from the Quarto Extensions registry, GitHub repositories, URLs, or local paths.
- **Shiny**: This is an extension to help launch [Shiny](https://shiny.posit.co) applications. Shiny is a package for Python and R that is designed to make it easy to build interactive web applications with the powerful data and scientific features of Python and R.

Some of them are pre-installed with Positron; other require opt-in installs via the *Extensions* panel.

## 7. Setup Python (optional)

In Positron:

- Open the palette with the keyboard shortcut `CMD + SHIFT + P`;
- Search for `Python: install Python via uv` and proceed.

More at <https://opensource.posit.co/blog/2026-07-08_positron-uv/>

## 8. Install Python packages (optional)

[uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) is an extremely fast Python package and project manager, written in Rust.

You can easily install Python packages in dedicated virtual environments with `uv`. For example, to install the `pandas` and `numpy` packages, run in the Positron-integrated terminal:

```bash
uv init example
# Initialized project `example` at `/home/user/example`
uv add pandas numpy
```

More details can be found on the website.

## 9. Version checks, all together

For these courses, we will use R and Quarto.

Run in the R console:

```r
R.version.string
```

and in a terminal:

```bash
quarto --version
```

If both report a version, you are ready. Ask the instructor for help if any
step errors; resolve these at the start so the labs run smoothly.
